extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (counsel) preparing jury instructions in U.S. patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for use in U.S. patent litigation that identify legal standards juries must apply (claim construction, infringement, invalidity, damages, willfulness, etc.) and provide drafting/customization guidance for judges and counsel. Intended as a neutral, precedentially-grounded set of instructions to be adapted to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge will define the meaning of the patent claims and instruct the jury on claim language; jurors must follow the court’s construction and must not define claims themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘It will be my job to tell you what the language of the patent claims means. You must follow my instructions as to the meaning of the patent claims. You are not to define the patent claims yourselves.’’ Use bracketed placeholders to adapt language to product vs. method contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction for the Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Case-specific construction of claim terms will be provided for the jury to use in comparing accused products/methods to claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions include a section titled 'Claim Construction for the Case' and may include alternate bracketed formulations to be customized to the particular claim terms and dispute in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of Means-Plus-Function Claims for the Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Special instruction for construction of means-plus-function (and step-plus-function) claims applicable to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes directions for identifying the corresponding structure/steps in the specification that perform the claimed function and instructs jurors how to apply that construction in infringement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Knowledge of the Patent and Intent Are Immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: For direct infringement, the defendant's knowledge of the patent and intent to infringe are immaterial to establishing liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction is separate from willfulness; jurors should not consider knowledge/intent when determining whether direct infringement occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Literal Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element (or method step) recited in that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must determine literal infringement with respect to each asserted patent claim individually. If the accused product/method does not contain one or more elements, it does not literally infringe that claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Joint Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions dealing with when multiple actors together may be found to directly infringe a claim (joint infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides standards for attributing steps or actions of multiple parties to a single actor for purposes of infringement, tailored to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal Infringement of Means-Plus-Function or Step-Plus-Function Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: How to assess literal infringement for means-plus-function (and analogous step-plus-function) claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires comparison of accused structure/steps to the structures or equivalents disclosed in the specification that perform the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of Dependent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: How to determine infringement of dependent claims (claims that add limitations to independent claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must evaluate dependent claims individually; dependent claims require that the accused product/method meet all limitations of the dependent claim (including the limitations of the claims on which they depend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of 'Comprising,' 'Consisting of,' and 'Consisting Essentially of' Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions on the different claim-open/closed language effects ('comprising' vs 'consisting of' vs 'consisting essentially of').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how these transitional phrases affect scope (e.g., 'comprising' is open-ended) and instructs jurors how to apply those meanings when comparing accused products/methods to claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement—Doctrine of Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is infringed under the doctrine of equivalents if the accused product/method contains an equivalent component/step for each claimed element not literally present; an equivalent is only insubstantially different (e.g., performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that each missing claim element has an equivalent in the accused product/method. Includes limitations discussed elsewhere (prosecution history estoppel; subject matter dedicated to the public).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Doctrine of Equivalents—Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents is limited by prosecution history estoppel when claim amendments or statements during prosecution surrender claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides jurors guidance on when prosecution history estoppel may bar equivalence and how to consider prosecution file history (file wrapper) evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Doctrine of Equivalents—Subject Matter Dedicated to the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents does not extend to subject matter that was dedicated to the public (e.g., disclaimed or surrendered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must consider whether features were dedicated to the public such that equivalence is barred for those aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively Inducing Patent Infringement (Inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard for liability when a party is accused of actively inducing others to infringe a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction addresses the elements of inducement (e.g., knowledge of the patent and intent to cause another to infringe) and must be tailored to the defendant’s conduct and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of All or Substantial Portion to Another Country (§ 271(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction applying 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(1) for supplying components of a patented invention for assembly abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the specific elements required under § 271(f)(1) and how to assess supply of components that constitute a substantial portion of the patented invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard for contributory infringement liability for supplying a component especially made for use in a patented invention and not suitable for substantial noninfringing use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes elements such as knowledge of the patent, component suitability, and lack of substantial noninfringing use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Supply of Components Especially Made or Adapted for Use in the Patented Invention into Another Country (§ 271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction applying 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2) for exporting components especially made/adapted for use in a patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out the requirements under § 271(f)(2) for foreign supply liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by Import, Sale, Offer for Sale or Use of Product Made by Patented Process (§ 271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction addressing liability under 35 U.S.C. § 271(g) for importation/sale/use of a product made by a patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the elements required to find liability for products made by a patented process and subsequently imported/sold/offered for sale or used in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Invalidity Defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must prove invalidity of each challenged claim by clear and convincing evidence to overcome the presumption of patent validity; invalidity is a defense to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains standard of proof differences: infringement by preponderance of the evidence; invalidity by clear and convincing evidence (‘‘highly probable’’ language recommended as a jury-friendly substitute). Practice Note discusses substituting 'highly probable' for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of prior art under pre-AIA law for §§ 102(a), (b), (d), (e), and (g) (e.g., date of invention, one-year bars, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: Cutoff Date under pre-AIA varies by subsection and may differ by claim; jurors may need instructions on determining Cutoff Date for each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of prior art under the America Invents Act (AIA): prior art is art effectively filed or published before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under AIA, Cutoff Date is the effective filing date of a claimed invention; provides contrast to pre-AIA definitions and notes that different claims may have different Cutoff Dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Considered or Not Considered by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction distinguishing prior art considered by the Patent Office during prosecution from other prior art and how jurors should treat evidence of what the PTO considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the prosecution history (file wrapper) and its relevance to invalidity and claim construction issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of Independent and Dependent Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: How to evaluate invalidity defenses applied to independent versus dependent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must assess invalidity for each challenged claim separately, accounting for claim dependencies and differing Cutoff Dates where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction defining the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) for purposes of obviousness, enablement, written description, and other patentability inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides factors for jurors to consider in assessing the level of ordinary skill (education, experience, typical practitioner background) and how that affects obviousness and enablement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation (novelty) requires that a single prior art reference disclose every element of the claimed invention such that the claim is not new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes multiple subtopics explaining forms of prior art and the required proof that a single reference meets all claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—Prior Public Knowledge (pre-AIA & AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: How prior public knowledge can serve as anticipation under pre-AIA and AIA regimes, with Cutoff Date distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate subsections for pre-AIA and AIA treatments (6.1.1 and 6.1.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—Prior Public Use (pre-AIA & AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior public use of an invention can anticipate a claim, with distinct rules pre-AIA and under AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsections explain evidentiary standards and differences between pre-AIA and AIA law applicable to public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—On-Sale Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale (or offer for sale) of an invention before the statutory cutoff can bar patentability; rules differ depending on pre-AIA vs AIA provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes discussion of experimental use exceptions and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—Experimental Use
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental-use exception to certain bars (e.g., on-sale) and how to evaluate whether pre-commercial activity was experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains factors distinguishing experimental activity from commercial activity that would trigger a bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—Printed Publication
rubrics_metrics.description: When a printed publication constitutes prior art that anticipates a claim (timing, public accessibility, content disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides standards for determining whether a document was sufficiently publicly accessible to be a printed publication and whether it discloses all claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation—Prior Patent and Earlier-Filed Patent Applications (pre-AIA & AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: How prior patents and earlier-filed patent applications can be prior art and anticipate claims; separate treatments for pre-AIA and AIA contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes distinctions for earlier-filed U.S. patent documents and foreign patent publications; addresses priority and effective filing date issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—Generally (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is assessed under the Graham framework: scope and content of prior art, differences between claimed invention and prior art, level of ordinary skill in the art, and secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction 'Obviousness—Generally' frames the analysis and directs jurors to evaluate the four factors and apply them together to determine whether the invention would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—First Factor: Scope and Content of the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention when analyzing obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should identify the prior art references most pertinent to the asserted claims and what they disclose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—Second Factor: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art references identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what, if anything, the claimed invention adds beyond the prior art and whether those differences would have been obvious to a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—Third Factor: Level of Ordinary Skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) in determining whether differences would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the defined POSITA attributes (education, experience) to evaluate whether a practitioner would have been motivated to combine references or modify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—Fourth Factor: Other Considerations (Secondary Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider objective indicia (secondary considerations) such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, copying, unexpected results, and industry praise in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness and must be considered where supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors evaluate whether the disclosure is sufficient in light of the POSITA; enablement is a separate ground of invalidity from anticipation/obviousness and written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must provide an adequate written description showing that the inventor possessed the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors assess whether the application as filed describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a POSITA would recognize the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal principles governing patent damages, including types of recoverable damages and starting date for damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction 'Damages—Generally' frames available remedies and principles such as apportionment and reasonable royalty analysis; includes Practice Notes and citations to cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin (Alternate A—Stipulated; Alternate B—Disputed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for determining the start date of damages period: Alternate A if parties stipulate start date; Alternate B if disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides alternative jury instruction language depending on whether the parties have stipulated the start date of infringement/damages; instructs jurors how to decide if disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—Kinds of Damages That May Be Recovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerates recoverable damages categories including lost profits, price erosion, cost escalation, convoyed sales, and reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category has a dedicated instruction explaining when it applies, elements required, and how to calculate damages (e.g., lost-profits causation, apportionment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction on awarding lost profits when a patent owner can show but-for sales lost to the infringer and meet the Primavera/ Panduit /other causation tests (i.e., demand for product, absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes, patent as the cause of lost sales, capacity to exploit demand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires proof that the patented feature drove customer demand (entire-market value rule only where patented feature is the basis for customer demand or substantially creates the value). Case citations provided (Ericsson, VirnetX, LaserDynamics, Uniloc, Lucent, Rite-Hite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Compensation for diminution of price the patentee could have charged as a result of infringement impacting pricing of the patentee’s product(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when price erosion theory is applicable and the evidence needed to support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for increased costs the patentee incurred because of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains measurement and evidentiary requirements for cost escalation damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed Sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for sales of non-patented products that are sold together with the patented product as a package or to the same customer base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when convoyed sales damages are recoverable and the causation/linkage required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Award based on what the parties would have agreed to in a hypothetical negotiation at the time infringement began (Georgia-Pacific framework and related considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes many subtopics: apportionment of value, treating multiple patents, timing of hypothetical negotiation, use of comparable licenses, availability of noninfringing substitutes, and that damages are not a hindsight evaluation but may consider what parties would have foreseen. Cites 35 U.S.C. § 284 and numerous Federal Circuit authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Multiple Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple patents are infringed, jurors may award separate royalties for each patent and consider the effect of multiple licenses on the hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors should account for number of licenses needed for the accused product and resulting effect on royalty rates (Ericsson, Apple v. Motorola, Verizon v. Vonage, Stickle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable royalty is determined at the time of the hypothetical negotiation, not by hindsight; but jurors may consider evidence parties would have foreseen (including some post-negotiation evidence in certain circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors may consider licenses entered shortly after negotiation, profits earned by infringer, and noninfringing alternatives if reasonably foreseeable at negotiation date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Availability of Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining royalty, jurors may consider availability and cost of acceptable noninfringing substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must be licensed under the patent or not infringe the patent (cites Prism Techs, Mars, Zygo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Use of Comparable License Agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors may consider amounts others paid for comparable licenses when estimating a reasonable royalty, but must adjust for differences between those licenses and the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License agreements need not be perfectly comparable; jurors must account for differences in technology and economic circumstances (Ericsson, Apple v. Motorola, LaserDynamics, ResQNet.com, Lucent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts Resolved Against Infringer (Damages Recordkeeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any doubts on damages arising from the defendant’s failure to keep proper records should be resolved in favor of the patent owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Bigelow, Story Parchment, Minco, Sensonics, Lam. Jury may resolve confusion or difficulties caused by defendant’s records against the defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard-Essential Patents (SEPs) and FRAND
rubrics_metrics.description: When SEPs and FRAND commitments are at issue, jurors must be instructed on the patentee’s FRAND commitments and on apportionment of value to the portion of the standard and to the claimed invention; only relevant Georgia‑Pacific factors should be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note: In SEP cases, courts must instruct on FRAND particulars and apportionment, and avoid instructing on irrelevant Georgia‑Pacific factors (citing Commw. Sci. & Indus. Research Org. v. Cisco and Ericsson v. D-Link).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is found, the jury must determine whether the infringement was willful; plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that defendant knew of the patent and intentionally infringed at least one asserted claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willfulness refers to conduct that may be malicious, wanton, deliberate, consciously wrongful, flagrant, or in bad faith; however, knowledge of the patent alone is insufficient to find willfulness. Jurors must assess all circumstances and the defendant’s knowledge at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement—Reliance on Legal Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how a defendant's reliance on a legal opinion may be considered as a factor in the willfulness inquiry if the defendant asserts such reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. § 298 bars using failure to obtain an opinion of counsel as evidence of willfulness, but if the defendant offers a competent legal opinion, jurors may consider reasonable reliance on it as part of the totality of circumstances. Instruction should be modified depending on whether defendant asserts reliance on counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and Standards of Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Different issues use different standards: infringement (preponderance of the evidence), invalidity (clear and convincing evidence), willfulness (preponderance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Note suggests substituting 'highly probable' to explain 'clear and convincing' to jurors. The instructions explain the spectrum: preponderance (~>50%), clear and convincing (between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt), beyond a reasonable doubt (criminal standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and Juror Conduct Instructions (Trial Phases and Evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary procedural instructions about the six phases of a jury trial, what opening statements and closing arguments are, how evidence is presented, and juror responsibilities (keep open mind, base decision on evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the phases (jury selection, opening statements, evidence presentation, closing arguments, final instructions, deliberations) and that opening/closing statements are not evidence; jurors must wait until all evidence is presented before deciding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customization Using Bracketed Terms and Practice Notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Model Instructions use bracketed terminology and Practice Notes to enable judges and counsel to customize the instructions to the specifics of a case (e.g., [the Plaintiff], [the Defendant], [allegedly infringing product], product vs method variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice Notes: brackets enable find-and-replace; replace 'system' with 'product' or 'method' with 'process' as appropriate. Practice Notes are not law but practical drafting guidance.
